content: SLPI, also known as secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor, is an enzyme encoded by the SLPI gene in humans. It is a highly cationic single-chain protein characterized by the presence of eight intramolecular disulfide bonds. This protein is abundantly present in the mucosal linings of the bronchi, cervix, and nasal passages, as well as in saliva and seminal fluids. SLPI functions as an inhibitor of several proteolytic enzymes, including human leukocyte elastase, cathepsin G, trypsin, neutrophil elastase, and mast cell chymase. Structural studies using X-ray crystallography have revealed that SLPI consists of two homologous domains, each comprising 53 and 54 amino acids. The C-terminal domain exhibits anti-protease activity, while the N-terminal domain has no known functional role. The SLPI gene encodes a secreted inhibitor that plays a critical role in protecting epithelial tissues from damage caused by serine proteases. It is found in various secretions, such as seminal plasma, cervical mucus, and bronchial secretions, and demonstrates a strong affinity for trypsin, leukocyte elastase, and cathepsin G. By inhibiting these proteases, SLPI contributes to the immune response by safeguarding epithelial surfaces from endogenous proteolytic enzyme attacks. Additionally, SLPI is believed to possess broad-spectrum antibiotic activity. Clinically, the SLPI gene is expressed in cells located at numerous mucosal surfaces, including those in the lungs, cervix, seminal vesicles, and parotid ducts. SLPI is one of the predominant proteins in nasal epithelial lining fluid and other nasal secretions. Its expression in tissues shows clear compartmentalization, with the highest levels observed in the endocervix and the lowest in the endometrium of postmenopausal women. Hormonal treatments can modulate SLPI expression along the reproductive tract. Several diseases, such as emphysema, cystic fibrosis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, are associated with elevated levels of neutrophil elastase. SLPI serves as a major defense mechanism against the destruction of pulmonary and epithelial tissues caused by neutrophil elastase. In secretions, SLPI is the primary elastase inhibitor, whereas α1-antitrypsin is the dominant elastase inhibitor in tissues. The pathogenesis of these diseases often results from the overwhelming of SLPI and α1-antitrypsin defenses by neutrophil elastase. Recombinant human SLPI has been proposed as a potential therapeutic agent for managing symptoms of cystic fibrosis, genetic emphysema, and asthma. Furthermore, SLPI levels are occasionally monitored to correlate with various pathological conditions. Elevated SLPI levels in nasal secretions and bronchoalveolar fluids may indicate inflammatory lung conditions or allergic reactions, while increased plasma levels may suggest pneumonia. Higher SLPI levels in saliva and plasma have also been linked to HIV infection, as evidenced by the near absence of HIV transmission through oral-to-oral contact. SLPI’s antiviral activity is attributed to its interference with protease-mediated events, such as viral entry into host cells and replication of viral genetic material. Studies have demonstrated that reduced SLPI levels in saliva correspond to decreased anti-HIV activity. Notably, SLPI exhibits anti-HIV properties under physiological conditions rather than artificial ones. Additionally, there is an inverse correlation between SLPI levels and high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, indicating that elevated SLPI levels provide protection against HPV infection. SLPI has been shown to interact with PLSCR1 and PLSCR4 on the plasma membrane of T-cells, particularly near CD4. This interaction is hypothesized to be one of the mechanisms by which SLPI inhibits HIV infection. Moreover, SLPI can bind to the Annexin A2/S100A10 heterotetramer (A2t), a co-factor for HIV infection, on the surface of macrophages. This interaction with A2t has also been demonstrated to block HPV uptake and infection of epithelial cells.
